The composite impact absorber studied is a prismatic sandwich structure with foam or honeycomb core and composite face plates.
Polyurethane foam is used for the core, while carbon, aramid, and glass fibers in thermosetting polymers are used for the faces.
Explicit finite element analysis was performed using LS-Dyna software.
Initial numerical results showed about 25% difference from experimental data in reaction force and absorbed energy.
Two methods to introduce initial imperfections were used: a tapered last ring of elements and small axial-symmetric transverse forces.
Introducing initial imperfections improved correlation with experimental results, reducing differences in peak force and energy absorbed to under 6%.
Compression speed affects peak reaction force and stiffness; higher speeds increase these values due to dynamic effects.
Lower compression speeds reduce peak force but increase computational time significantly.
Material model type 55 in LS-Dyna, implementing Tsai-Wu failure criteria, was found most suitable for simulating the composite absorber.
Contact modeling included tied surface-to-surface contact for adhesion and eroding contact pairs to simulate failure.
Foam material properties have minor influence on absorber behavior compared to composite face properties.
Energy absorption occurs through localized crushing of the core and bending/stretching of the face plates.
The test case geometry included a 450 mm core thickness and 2 mm laminated face thickness.
Numerical analyses considered a compression speed of 10 m/s initially, then lower speeds for comparison.
Differences in numerical and experimental results were attributed to absence of natural imperfections and higher numerical compression speed.
Six contact pairs were defined to simulate interactions between foam, laminates, and impact plates.
The study performed a sensitivity analysis on geometric and material parameters affecting energy absorption.
The numerical model calibration was based on experimental data from literature, specifically from Mamalis et al. (2002).
The reaction force vs. displacement curves were used to compare numerical and experimental results.
The study concluded that initial imperfections and compression speed are critical parameters for accurate modeling.
